title: A Player's Motives Criticised in a Specimen Game
subtitle: A plan must fit the position and involve all the pieces

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter IV, §25 A Player's Motives Criticised in a Specimen Game, Example 55

narration.say: Alexander plays White against Sir George Thomas. We will examine not just the moves, but the plans behind them.
Both sides develop. Black chooses a setup with the knight on d7 and the queen on a5.
White exchanges bishop for knight. Black brings the other knight to e4.
White moves the queen to b3. Black develops the bishop to e7.
Capablanca criticises the bishop's square: d6 would have been a more purposeful post.

steps.title: The pawn advance changes the plan

narration.say: White develops the bishop to d3. Black exchanges the knight on c3 and then the central pawn.
Black brings the bishop to f6. Both sides castle.
White advances e4, and Black answers e5.
White plays d5. This limits the bishop on c4 and gives Black time to develop the bishop on c8.
Black moves the queen to c7. White retreats the bishop to d3, and Black begins developing the queenside.
White brings the rook from f1 to c1. Black redirects the bishop through e7 to c5.
Queen to b2. Black plays f6.
Capablanca criticises this phase of Black's play for lacking a strong, well-defined plan. Having good pieces is not enough: they need a common objective.
White moves the rook to b1. Black centralises a rook, while the bishop moves to a6.
White returns the rook to d1. Black doubles on the central files.
The queen goes to b3. Black lifts the rook to d6.
White moves the knight to h4. Black plays g6, and White retreats the bishop to e2.

steps.title: A strong-looking move can obstruct your own pieces

narration.say: Black exchanges on d5. White recaptures with the e-pawn.
Black advances e4. White plays g3.
Black pushes on to e3. The pawn looks dangerous, but Capablanca criticises the advance because it blocks the bishop on c5.
A pawn advance needs coordinated support. An isolated threat can make the opponent's position safer instead of breaking it.
White advances f4. Black reroutes the other bishop to f5.
White puts the rook on b2. Black brings the rook to e4.
White moves the king to g2. Black brings the queen to c8, and White retreats the knight to g1.
Black advances g5. The pawn exchange opens more lines.
White brings the rook to f1. Black advances g4.
White retreats the bishop to d3. Black shifts the rook from d6 to f6.
The knight goes to e2. Black brings the queen to f8, supporting the attack.
White withdraws the rook from b2 to b1. Black brings the queen to h6, and White moves the queen to c2.
Black's queen can penetrate to h3. Follow Thomas's attacking plan.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Bring the queen to h3.

feedback.*: Queen to h3 checks the king on g2 and brings the attack closer.

exercise.success: 39...Qh3+! White moves the king to h1.

steps.title: A rook sacrifice with a purpose
steps.source: Black therefore tries to get the Queen away from the defence. A very beautiful move, and the best way to carry on the attack.

narration.say: The white queen helps defend the position. Black offers a rook to draw it away.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Sacrifice the rook by taking the pawn on c4.

feedback.*: The rook on e4 can capture c4. The sacrifice tempts White's queen away from its defensive duties.

narration.say: Black takes the bishop on d3. White captures the rook on f6, and Black takes the queen on c4.
White moves the knight to f4. The queen on h3 is attacked by the pawn on g3, but Black has a more urgent threat.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Advance the passed pawn with a threat of promotion.

feedback.*: Push the pawn from e3 to e2. White must answer the promotion threat instead of taking the queen.

exercise.success: 43...e2! White has no time to capture the queen.

steps.title: The attack reaches the back rank

narration.say: Queen to f1. The queen is supported by the pawn on e2, and Black threatens promotion with checkmate. White resigns.

steps.title: Judge the plan, not just the move

narration.say: Capablanca criticises both players when their moves lack a clear strategic purpose.
The advance to e3 was premature because it obstructed a bishop. Later, coordinated support made that same pawn decisive.
The final attack combined queen pressure, a rook sacrifice, bishop captures and a promotion threat.
A move is not strong merely because it creates a threat. It must fit a plan that your available pieces can carry out.
